articles.title: A Tennessee company is breaking down retired wind turbine blades instead of sending them to landfills, recovering glass fibre at 99.9% purity that can be reused in concrete, car panels and 3D-printing filament
articles.summary: US News: Retired wind turbine blades are becoming a growing waste challenge as older turbines reach the end of their operating lives, but a Tennessee company i.
articles.body: Retired wind turbine blades are becoming a growing waste challenge as older turbines reach the end of their operating lives, but a Tennessee company is developing a way to recover valuable material from them instead of sending the blades to landfill. Carbon Rivers, a Knoxville-based advanced materials company, uses a heat-based process to separate glass fibre from the polymers and resins that hold turbine blades together. The US Department of Energy has reported that the company achieved 99.9% purity in recovered glass fibre, creating the possibility of using the material again in products such as composite panels, construction materials and 3D-printing filament. The technology has received millions of dollars in federal support and research collaboration with the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. Rather than treating an old blade as waste, the process aims to turn its materials into feedstock for new manufacturing.How a Tennessee company is recycling retired wind turbine bladesCarbon Rivers is tackling one of the hardest parts of wind turbine recycling by targeting the composite material used in the blades. The US Department of Energy estimates that around 85% to 90% of a wind turbine's mass can already be recycled, with steel, copper and other materials having established recycling routes. The remaining fraction is much more difficult because turbine blades are made from fibre-reinforced composites, in which glass fibres are embedded in tough polymer resins. Those materials are designed to resist fatigue, weather and repeated mechanical stress, but the same durability makes them difficult to separate at the end of their service life. Carbon Rivers uses a process known as pyrolysis, which heats the composite in the absence of oxygen so that the organic resin and polymer components break down while the inorganic glass fibres remain. The recovered fibres can then be cleaned and processed for reuse. The approach is intended to preserve more of the material's value than simply grinding blades into waste or using them in low-value applications.The recycling process works by exploiting the different behaviour of organic and inorganic materials when exposed to intense heat. During pyrolysis, the polymer components of the blade decompose without oxygen, producing hydrocarbon products including syngas and pyrolysis oil. Carbon Rivers can recover these materials for energy-related uses while separating the glass fibre reinforcement from the composite. Once separated, the fibre can be cleaned and prepared for manufacturing applications. The US Department of Energy reported that Carbon Rivers achieved 99.9% recycled glass fibre purity, a level that could allow the recovered material to be used in applications that would otherwise require virgin fibreglass. Carbon Rivers describes its technology as Glass to Glass reclamation, with the aim of taking glass-fibre composites at the end of their useful life and returning the recovered fibre to manufacturing. The process has also been investigated for other composite waste streams, including materials from the automotive and marine industries, suggesting that the technology could eventually address a broader waste problem rather than being limited to wind turbine blades.The recovered material can be used in new productsThe biggest potential advantage of recovering the glass fibre is that it can be turned into useful manufacturing material rather than simply disposed of. DOE has identified applications including non-woven mats, continuous textile yarns, thermoplastic pellets, automotive sheet-moulding compounds and filament for 3D printing. Recovered glass fibre can also be incorporated into construction materials and potentially remelted or blended with virgin fibreglass for other uses. This creates the possibility of a more circular system in which the material from an old turbine blade becomes part of another product instead of ending up in a landfill. Carbon Rivers has also worked on applications beyond wind energy, including automotive, marine and structural composite materials. That matters because glass-fibre composites are used in many industries, creating a much larger potential market for recovered material. The technology could eventually allow manufacturers to use recycled glass fibre in products such as vehicle panels, building components and other composite products while reducing their dependence on newly manufactured fibreglass.Millions in government funding helped scale the technologyCarbon Rivers' technology has received substantial support from the US Department of Energy. DOE reported that the company received approximately $2.4 million through its Wind Energy Technologies Office and Small Business Technology Transfer programme beginning in 2019, with researchers at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, working with the company to scale up the recovery process. By 2022, DOE said Carbon Rivers had upcycled more than 100 tons of wind turbine blade material into products such as non-woven mats, thermoplastic pellets and 3D-printing filament. A later DOE report said the company had processed a few thousand metric tons and was working towards much greater processing capacity. In 2023, the company also received a $1.1 million Phase III award through DOE's wind-energy technology programme to further develop the recycling process and support the use of recovered glass fibre in new composite applications. DOE has described the work as an example of technology development moving from research towards commercialisation. The government support is particularly significant because recycling old blades requires not only a technically effective process but also enough capacity to handle large and irregular waste streams generated by the wind industry.Tennessee could help build a more circular wind industryCarbon Rivers is based in Knoxville, Tennessee, and its recycling work has been linked to plans for a larger facility in nearby Kingston. The original DOE announcement described plans for a facility at a historic site associated with the Manhattan Project and said it was expected to process thousands of wind turbine blades each year. Those original projections should not be treated as confirmation that the facility opened on schedule, but they illustrate the scale the company was targeting as it moved from pilot work towards commercial processing. The broader need is clear. DOE says most of a wind turbine can already be recycled, but composite blades remain a major challenge, and many retired blades still go to landfill because recycling capacity and economics remain limited. Carbon Rivers is one of several companies and research groups working to change that situation. Its process does not mean every old turbine blade can now be recycled cheaply or indefinitely, but recovering high-purity glass fibre creates another route for keeping valuable material in circulation. If the technology can be scaled economically, retired blades could become a source of manufacturing feedstock for construction, automotive products, 3D printing and potentially new wind turbine components, helping reduce the amount of composite waste sent to landfill as the wind industry continues to expand.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. The process has also been investigated for other composite waste streams, including materials from the automotive and marine industries, suggesting that the technology could eventually address a broader waste problem rather than being limited to wind turbine blades.The recovered material can be used in new productsThe biggest potential advantage of recovering the glass fibre is that it can be turned into useful manufacturing material rather than simply disposed of. DOE has identified applications including non-woven mats, continuous textile yarns, thermoplastic pellets, automotive sheet-moulding compounds and filament for 3D printing. Recovered glass fibre can also be incorporated into construction materials and potentially remelted or blended with virgin fibreglass for other uses. This creates the possibility of a more circular system in which the material from an old turbine blade becomes part of another product instead of ending up in a landfill. Carbon Rivers has also worked on applications beyond wind energy, including automotive, marine and structural composite materials. That matters because glass-fibre composites are used in many industries, creating a much larger potential market for recovered material. The technology could eventually allow manufacturers to use recycled glass fibre in products such as vehicle panels, building components and other composite products while reducing their dependence on newly manufactured fibreglass.Millions in government funding helped scale the technologyCarbon Rivers' technology has received substantial support from the US Department of Energy. DOE reported that the company received approximately $2.4 million through its Wind Energy Technologies Office and Small Business Technology Transfer programme beginning in 2019, with researchers at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, working with the company to scale up the recovery process. By 2022, DOE said Carbon Rivers had upcycled more than 100 tons of wind turbine blade material into products such as non-woven mats, thermoplastic pellets and 3D-printing filament. A later DOE report said the company had processed a few thousand metric tons and was working towards much greater processing capacity. In 2023, the company also received a $1.1 million Phase III award through DOE's wind-energy technology programme to further develop the recycling process and support the use of recovered glass fibre in new composite applications. DOE has described the work as an example of technology development moving from research towards commercialisation. The government support is particularly significant because recycling old blades requires not only a technically effective process but also enough capacity to handle large and irregular waste streams generated by the wind industry.Tennessee could help build a more circular wind industryCarbon Rivers is based in Knoxville, Tennessee, and its recycling work has been linked to plans for a larger facility in nearby Kingston. The original DOE announcement described plans for a facility at a historic site associated with the Manhattan Project and said it was expected to process thousands of wind turbine blades each year. Those original projections should not be treated as confirmation that the facility opened on schedule, but they illustrate the scale the company was targeting as it moved from pilot work towards commercial processing. The broader need is clear. DOE says most of a wind turbine can already be recycled, but composite blades remain a major challenge, and many retired blades still go to landfill because recycling capacity and economics remain limited. Carbon Rivers is one of several companies and research groups working to change that situation. Its process does not mean every old turbine blade can now be recycled cheaply or indefinitely, but recovering high-purity glass fibre creates another route for keeping valuable material in circulation. If the technology can be scaled economically, retired blades could become a source of manufacturing feedstock for construction, automotive products, 3D printing and potentially new wind turbine components, helping reduce the amount of composite waste sent to landfill as the wind industry continues to expand.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Cases in the US have hit the highest point since the virus was eliminated, as vaccination rates decline.
articles.body:
Two people who were not vaccinated against measles have died of the virus in Pennsylvania, health officials said.

The state has seen 393 cases of the highly contagious virus this year, as infections across the US have hit the highest point in 35 years.

Eighty-five percent of kindergarten-age students in Lancaster County, where the recent deaths occurred, are vaccinated against measles - well below the 95% rate needed for herd immunity to limit the spread and protect immunocompromised people.

Last year, two unvaccinated children in Texas died from a measles outbreak that infected over 1,000 people, primarily children.

"This is a serious and a growing problem across our country and in our commonwealth," Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said in a news conference on Tuesday. "This illness and death from measles is completely preventable."

He added that the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) vaccine was the best tool to protect against illness and death.

Officials said they would not share any additional information on the identities of those who died, including if they were children, who have face a higher risk of death and complications from measles.

The US has seen 2,777 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, just seven months into the year, up from last year's high of 2,289.

The rising number of cases comes as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates. The US recommends two shots to children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that calls for fewer childhood vaccinations and recommends splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots. Public health experts worry the order will cause confusion about an already safe and effective vaccine and prove costly.

The executive order came after Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr took a number of steps to remake US vaccine policies over the past year, including the childhood vaccination schedule. Many of the changes were blocked by a federal judge earlier this year.

A vaccine skeptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, at times endorsing it and other times sharing unproven claims about its safety.

Speaking on Tuesday, Shapiro said he spoke with Kennedy over the phone that morning and that he had offered to send staff from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Shapiro said he was "very blunt" with Kennedy about vaccinations.

"I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that's coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America ... that there's real life consequences to spreading misinformation," Shapiro said.

The US is on track to lose its status of having eliminated measles, which will be determined by a panel in November. Canada lost its status last year.

articles.title: A New Jersey artist bought a 600-square-foot cabin in 1989 and kept adding to it; 37 years later, Luna Parc is a 5,000-square-foot home, studio and living artwork still being built
articles.summary: US News: When Ricky Boscarino came across a small 600-square-foot cabin in the woods in New Jersey in 1988, he saw more than just a place to live. A year later.
articles.body: When Ricky Boscarino came across a small 600-square-foot cabin in the woods in New Jersey in 1988, he saw more than just a place to live. A year later, he began transforming it into what would become his largest work in progress called Luna Parc.More than three decades later, the property in Sandyston Township has grown into a 5,000-square-foot home, studio and working art environment. According to SPACES Archives, the property now has 11 levels and 15 rooms, with each part reflecting Boscarino's work as an artist and craftsman.Boscarino, also known as Ricky of Luna Parc, comes from an artistic family. His family history, according to the Luna Parc website, goes back to the time of the Medici. He has continued that connection through his own work in metal, clay, glass, wood and cement.He graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1982. His interest in creating unusual and detailed objects had developed much earlier. As a young student, he was recognised for making carefully crafted dioramas, including scenes of cockroaches in beauty salons and nativity scenes.Cabin became life-sized artworkBoscarino started transforming the New Jersey cabin in 1989. What began as a 600-square-foot structure eventually became a much larger space that combines his home and atelier.SPACES Archives describes Luna Parc as a personal home, working studio, living classroom and community artist space. The property has continued to develop as Boscarino has added new elements and used different materials and objects throughout the site.The entrance itself reflects this approach. A ferrocement structure welcomes visitors to the property and has been named the 'Artichoke Portico' by Boscarino.Inside, the rooms have their own themes and collections. The kitchen, for example, is decorated with milk tabs and nearly 20,000 wine corks placed along the walls. Other spaces include the Hall of Hats, Nature Lab, a weaving studio, a mosaiced bathroom and the Asia Room.The Asia Room contains a set of doors that are almost 200 years old. These objects are part of the wider collection that Boscarino has built into the property over the years.Objects from around the worldBoscarino is both an artist and a collector. He has travelled to more than 40 countries and brought back a practice or item from each place, incorporating them into Luna Parc.One of the spaces inside the home is the Ballroom. It contains Morse code messages, a real human skeleton and painted portraits created by Boscarino.The Ballroom is used to host artists and students for lectures and readings about different ways of working as an artist.As the house rises upwards, the spaces continue to change. Boscarino's bedroom is on the seventh level. At the top is the Sky Walk, decorated with whirlygigs and kinetic sculptures.From the Sky Walk, there is a view across the property and the garden. The outdoor area includes a cobalt blue bottle house and a garden designed to light up at night.There is also a small purple chapel on the property. It is surrounded by a fence made from crutches that Boscarino created in honour of his grandfather.The Chapel of the Saints and the crutch fence commemorate an event that Boscarino's grandfather witnessed as a child. According to the SPACES account, his grandfather saw a young man regain the ability to walk in front of him.Young artists learn at Luna ParcThe property is not only Boscarino's home and studio. Beyond the garden and chapel is his Atelier, where he works with interns who are young local artists.The programme gives them an opportunity to learn his techniques and craft. It also aims to show them another way of living and working as an artist.This part of Luna Parc became more formally organised in 2015, when Boscarino established the Luna Parc Atelier Foundation Inc. The foundation is an official non-profit.The foundation's programme also focuses on helping apprentices develop practical skills. According to the Luna Parc website, it âteaches apprentices hand working and business skills necessary to succeed as self-supporting artists,â while also caring for the home and its future.Luna Parc is not generally open to the public for tours. SPACES notes that visits are limited to certain Open House days.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Analysis: With UNIFIL set to leave, Lebanon seeks U.N.-backed successor
articles.summary: Lebanon wants to preservie a United Nations role in the south after the current peacekeeping force leaves, Lebanese and Western analysts said.
articles.body:
BEIRUT, Lebanon, Aug. 25 (UPI) -- Lebanon, struggling to secure an Israeli withdrawal from occupied parts of southern Lebanon and restore its sovereignty, is facing another challenge: preserving a United Nations role in the south after the current peacekeeping force leaves, Lebanese and Western analysts said.

Without an U.N.-mandated international presence, Lebanon risks losing an important source of protection and leverage and could find itself increasingly at the mercy of Israel and the United States -- the two countries that have pushed hardest to terminate the U.N. peacekeeping mission.

The issue is gaining urgency, as the mandate of the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL -- originally established after Israel's first invasion of southern Lebanon in 1978 to help confirm an Israeli withdrawal and assist the Lebanese government in re-establishing its authority -- is to expire at the end of this year.

Ironically, UNIFIL, tasked with maintaining peace in southern Lebanon for nearly five decades, is scheduled to leave as Lebanon once again negotiates -- this time through U.S.-brokered direct talks with Israel -- a new Israeli withdrawal and the future security of its southern territory.

Fearing a potential vacuum after multinational peacekeepers depart, Lebanon -- backed by a petition signed by 86 parliamentarians -- is pushing to keep UNIFIL in place, despite knowing that the effort will face opposition from Israel and the United States, while simultaneously seeking support for a replacement force under U.N. auspices.

Israel has strongly criticized UNIFIL for failing to fulfill its mission, accusing the force of allowing Hezbollah to strengthen its military presence in southern Lebanon since the 2006 war -- in violation of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701. It is therefore unlikely to agree to any U.N. role in the future.

For the United States, terminating UNIFIL's role fits within President Donald Trump's broader efforts to sideline the U.N. and diminish its role in addressing global crises. Washington also appears to favor a new mechanism outside the existing U.N. framework.

However, blaming UNIFIL for the situation in southern Lebanon overlooks the complex realities on the ground, as well as the responsibilities of the warring parties and the international community.

Lebanese retired Maj. Gen. Abdul Rahman Chehaitli, who previously served as a liaison officer between the Lebanese government and UNIFIL, said Israel and Hezbollah have been preparing for their next confrontation since the 2006 war, rather than demobilizing or laying the groundwork for lasting peace.

While Israel was strengthening its intelligence, targeting, defensive and ground war capabilities along its northern front, Hezbollah was rebuilding and expanding its military capabilities, including weapons stockpiles, defensive positions and underground infrastructure in southern Lebanon in anticipation of another Israeli invasion.

"All the countries were seeing these preparations," Chehaitli told UPI, dismissing Gaza and Iran as "superficial pretexts" for the wars and escalations between Hezbollah and Israel in 2023 and 2026.

He noted that UNIFIL, which grew significantly in size and scope after the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, "did not fail in its mission, but rather carried out its duties," intervening directly on numerous occasions to prevent military escalations.

But, he said, the peacekeeping force could not stop a war once either side had made the decision to fight, adding, "It cannot prevent a war made by a decision."

Chehaitli, who was involved in post-2026 negotiations on the implementation of Resolution 1701 aimed at ending hostilities, said UNIFIL also played a role in managing border disputes between Lebanon and Israel and assisting the Lebanese Army and residents of southern Lebanon.

However, the challenges facing UNIFIL were numerous, reflecting the limitations of its mandate and the powers it was actually given.

UNIFIL spokesperson Kandice Ardiel said the role of peacekeepers has never been to enforce Resolution 1701, but to support the parties, monitor and report on its implementation.

"The main challenge has always been the incomplete commitment by Lebanon and Israel implementing their obligations under Security Council resolutions," Ardiel told UPI. "Over the years, continued violations have undermined trust and complicated efforts to achieve lasting stability."

She also cited the challenges posed by conflict, unauthorized weapons in southern Lebanon and the Israeli presence north of the Blue Line -- the U.N.-identified line of withdrawal used to confirm Israel's pullout -- as well as restrictions on peacekeepers' freedom of movement and attacks against them.

However, Ardiel emphasized UNIFIL's "important contribution" to security and stability along the Blue line for almost 17 years thanks to the peacekeepers' "visible presence," liaison and coordination role to help prevent unintended escalation during periods of tension.

"From 2006 to 2023, the Blue Line saw the longest period of relative stability in recent history, allowing a whole generation of young people to grow up there without knowing conflict," she said.

Israel's intensive military campaign has killed 8,915 people and wounded 30,543 since October 8, 2023, according to a tally released by Lebanon's Ministry of Information last Friday. It caused massive destruction to property and infrastructure, with some 70 border villages in southern Lebanon reduced to rubble and rendered uninhabitable.

An important aspect of UNIFIL's mission has been the impartial recording of what happens on the ground, including violations by the parties. Its departure, therefore, would mean losing a credible witness whose reports provide an independent record of events and violations in southern Lebanon.

As the recent war revealed the extent of Hezbollah's military presence south of the Litani River, including an extensive network of underground tunnels, questions emerged over whether -- and to what extent -- UNIFIL should be held responsible.

Ardiel said U.N. peacekeepers had, over the years, reported locations and activities of concern to the Lebanese authorities and the Security Council, noting that they "had detected and reported suspected tunnel infrastructure" before the escalation of the conflict in late 2023. However, they were not authorized to enter private property without the necessary permission.

Hezbollah, for its part, would mobilize civilian supporters to block their access, a practice that became increasingly common, according to observers.

David Wood, a senior Lebanon analyst at the International Crisis Group, emphasized that UNIFIL never had a mandate to actively enforce disarmament by confronting Hezbollah. Rather, its role was to support the Lebanese Army, which, "for its own reasons," has not sought to confront Hezbollah or force it to withdraw from the area south of the Litani River.

In fact, the Lebanese Army needed the go-ahead from the political authorities, which for years supported Hezbollah's powerful armed presence and its claim to maintain an armed resistance, according to observers.

Today, Lebanon's new leadership is keen to restore its sovereignty at a time when Hezbollah has been significantly weakened by the war, while Israel has shown little willingness to relinquish the military upper hand and gains it achieved during its campaign against the Iran-backed group.

However, ending the war and securing Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon would require an international force on the ground -- a replacement for UNIFIL that Lebanon is discussing with European powers.

According to Wood, by far the preferable course for any new international force would be to operate under a U.N. Security Council mandate, providing "international legitimacy and backing to protect the (participating) troops," while also securing Israeli and U.S. consent.

Chehaitli warned that any new force without international cover or authority grounded in international law would leave Lebanon "at the mercy" of the United States and Israel, which "is now treating Lebanon as a weak country and imposing its conditions on it."

"UNIFIL used to put Lebanon at the same level of Israel, not as Lebanon is weak and Israel is strong, and used to be not only a witness but also a referee," he said.

He expressed concern that a new force without a U.N. mandate could face conflicts of interest among its participating countries and risk pushing Lebanon to the margins of international attention.

articles.title: U.K. estate used as Wayne Manor in "Batman Begins" must be surveyed for bats
articles.summary: Since being built in the 1850s, Mentmore Towers has been featured in "Batman Begins" and other movies, but has fallen into disrepair.
articles.body:
A British estate used as a filming location in Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" may be taken from its owners if repair work, including bat surveys, does not commence, according to local council notices.

The stately home was built between 1852 and 1854 in Buckinghamshire, a region in southeast England. It stood in for Wayne Manor in the 2005 superhero blockbuster, which starred Christian Bale and Katie Holmes .

Buckinghamshire Council served the company that owns the estate with a formal listed-buildings repair notice amid reports of deteriorating conditions at the property. CBS News partner BBC News reported that the notice was dated Aug. 4.

The building could be placed on the market – unless the owners show evidence that a licensed bat ecologist has been appointed to conduct surveys. The owners have one month to begin the process and provide evidence, council deputy leader Peter Strachan told CBS News. If the notice is not dealt with, the council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion, though this would be subject to further legal action, according to the BBC.

Mentmore Towers is considered a Grade I heritage building, which means it must have a special architectural or historical interest. Around 2.5% of buildings in the United Kingdom, including Buckingham Palace and the Tower of London, are among the Grade I-listed buildings that have been preserved.

The property has been owned by Mentmore Towers Limited since 1999. That company is owned by Simon Halabi, a Syrian-British property developer. In 2007, Halabi was named Britain's 14th richest man, according to The Times . However, in 2010, the tycoon was declared bankrupt over a $76 million loan he received from a failed Icelandic bank .

In addition to being used in "Batman Begins," Mentmore Towers was also featured in other films, including "The Mummy Returns" and "Johnny English." It was also used as a filming location in the Spice Girls' music video for the 1998 song "Goodbye." Before appearing onscreen, it was home to the Rothschild family. But despite its famous past, the building has "fallen into an increasingly worsening state of disrepair over recent years," the council told CBS News.

Historic England, a public body responsible for advising the government on protecting historic sites, lists the building as being in "very bad" condition and at risk of "further rapid deterioration." The organization noted that Mentmore Towers is on its Heritage at Risk register, "which identifies sites most at risk of being lost through neglect, decay or inappropriate development."

The BBC describes the building as having deteriorating roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork. According to Save Britain's Heritage , an independent charity that works to protect and restore historic buildings in England, permissions to repair the roof were granted in 2016, but the work was not completed.

The ecological survey is the first step of the repair work. By August 2027, the property owners must have conducted three such surveys, as well as acquired any essential historical licenses to undertake the necessary repairs.

The BBC reported that the owners must demonstrate that they are taking steps to appoint a contractor with appropriate experience for repairing listed buildings and roofs that are of similar size and historic appearance. Once repair work begins, Buckinghamshire Council and Historic England officers must be allowed to inspect it weekly, the BBC reported.

"We welcome this action taken by Buckinghamshire Council requiring the current owner to carry out urgent and overdue repairs to this great house," said Henrietta Billings, the director of Save Britain's Heritage. "We urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs. This exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long."

articles.title: NYC mom survives neck-slash attack on hiking trip in Arizona: 'I can’t die like this'
articles.summary: Ring camera footage captures New York City mother Alexis Rowan fighting for her life after a stranger slashed her neck on an Arizona birthday hike.
articles.body: A birthday hiking trip of a lifetime wound up being a death-defying fight for her life for a New York City mother of two, leaving her neck slashed, her hand stabbed, as well as physical and emotional scars that left 13 stitches and a nightmare that will never be forgotten. Alexis Rowan, 27, survived the northern Arizona mountain-hike attack only because of screams that were heard by a woman in a nearby home, forcing the suspect to flee, harrowing doorbell camera footage showed. "I was like, oh my God, my neck: I can't die like this, this is not the way," Alexis Rowan told WABC after returning to New York City after last week's ordeal on a tourist mountain hike in Arizona. "I have my kids to go home to." NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' Graphic photos shared by the New York Post showed the deep slash left on her neck and the 10 stitches that closed it, along with three more from being stabbed in the hand. She never wants "to look at another mountain again," she told the Post, while the lasting scar will remind her of the horror with every look in the mirror. On the Wednesday, Aug. 19, hike at the Havasupai Indian Reservation – just one day after her 27th birthday – Alexis was left briefly behind a friend when the suspect approached. The suspect, identified as Taylor Nardo Paya, 29, is a Havasupai tribe member with a rap sheet that included a guilty plea to assault, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL "It was the first person that I've seen in the village, and I said, 'Hey, excuse me, is that the gift shop?'" Rowan told WABC in one of the few interviews she granted. Fox News Digital reached out to her and her mother for an interview, but they have yet to respond. "I kept walking, I went to go in and that's when he just came up from behind," she continued, "and as soon as I felt my neck, I'm like, 'oh my God, I'm going to die.'" Footage showed Rowan fighting for her life as she was dragged by the hair from the ground – with her screams finally bringing a woman to open the door and causing the suspect to flee. The video obtained by Fox News Digital did not have the sound of the screams, but they were key to the suspect fleeing, according to reports. REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF COLLEGE STUDENT’S MURDER WAS KNOWN ‘THREAT’ AFTER PRIOR ARREST: VICTIM’S MOM "I'm just so grateful for the woman that opened the door that heard her screams; it's something you can never unhear," Tricia Rowan, Alexis' mother, told WABC of the "angel sent from heaven" woman who opened the door to help. "She's a fighter. She fought to make sure she's coming home to her babies, and she's my baby. So I'm so glad she made it, Tricia Rowan said. "He picked the wrong one. My daughter is a fighter, she is a warrior. She wasn’t going to take it." SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS Alexis Rowan told the Post she was "mentally aware" of the "danger" after her initial interaction with Paya. "My gut instinct was like, ‘This is not OK. I’m not OK,’" she said, adding that the "next person may not be as strong, may not be prepared mentally that someone is going to attack them or able to put them in danger." Reservation police located Paya the following day by pinging Rowan’s phone, which prosecutors say he allegedly stole after it fell from one of her backpacks. WOMAN ALLEGEDLY CHOKED SUBWAY RIDER, YELLED ANTISEMITIC REMARKS IN ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO: POLICE He was arrested and later taken into federal custody because the alleged attack occurred on tribal land, according to reports. Video obtained by Fox News Digital showed Paya being cuffed and taken away on a golf cart by federal police before another video showed him in an orange jumpsuit being perp-walked to a helicopter. Paya faces a federal assault with a deadly weapon charge, according to FOX 10. Court records show Paya pleaded guilty in 2016 to robbing and assaulting another woman in a 2015 attack, for which he received a five-year prison sentence and was ordered to undergo sex offender treatment and counseling. FIVE PLEAD GUILTY TO CHARGES IN BRUTAL CINCINNATI BEATDOWN THAT WENT VIRAL LAST SUMMER The victim's mother wants to see the perpetrator locked up indefinitely. "People are evil," she told the Post, calling him "a threat to society" and someone "you cannot rehabilitate." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There is no place on earth that they belong," she added, "other than behind bars like an animal in a cage because they’re predators and they prey on innocent victims."

articles.title: 'We got this wrong': Target says sorry for Halloween costume that looked like racist caricature, pulls it down from collection
articles.summary: US News: Target acknowledged and corrected its mistake after one of its children Hallowen costume triggered a massive outrage. The retain giant said it had pul.
articles.body: Target acknowledged and corrected its mistake after one of its children Hallowen costume triggered a massive outrage. The retain giant said it had pulled down the costume from sale after social media users pointed out that the circus clown evoked Blackface and minstrel shows."The $25 costume was listed as the âKidsâ Glows under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume Bodysuitâ from Targetâs Hyde & EEK! Boutique line. The design featured an orange-and-black clown outfit, black gloves and a dark face covering with an exaggerated smiling mouth. We still shopping at Target?" a social media post said, pointing out how problematic the Halloween costume was."As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry. The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale," Target said in its statement."We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this wonât happen again," the statement read.Social media was divided on whether it was an unintentional mistake. "At this point, it's intentional. There is no way no one on the board doesn't know this is offensive," one wrote. "Target definitely did this intentionally. Their marketing team is trying to stir up controversy. Even bad publicity is STILL publicity," another wrote.Blackface is dark makeup worn to mimic the appearance of a Black person and especially to mock or ridicule Black people, according to Merriam-Webster. The use of blackface in the US was recorded through âminstrel shows,â in which white performers would wear blackface and mock Black people.The Halloween costume controversy comes nearly a year after Target rolled back Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) initiatives.Internal email sent by chief merchandising officerChief merchandising officer of Target Cara Sylvester sent an internal email in which the employees were told that the iten should never have been in the assortment and that the company would learn from this and do better.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Of 27 lakh âlogical discrepancyâ deletions in West Bengal, only 7 lakh appealed
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a new twist to the simmering controversy over the West Bengal SIR, Supreme Court was informed Tuesday that against 27-lakh odd deletions.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a new twist to the simmering controversy over the West Bengal SIR, Supreme Court was informed Tuesday that against 27-lakh odd deletions from votersâ list because of âlogical discrepancyâ only seven lakh filed appeals seeking inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was informed by senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan that of total 38.1 lakh appeals filed before the SIR appellate tribunals, an overwhelming 31 lakh were filed by those who challenged inclusion of names in the rolls claiming they were ineligible to be voters in Bengal.Chunk of WB appeals was against inclusionThis was new information for SC, which was concerned by pendency of 37 lakh appeals, as 19 tribunals in last four months decided only 82,000 appeals. The new turn means 20 lakh of 27-lakh-odd voters deleted for logical discrepancy have not appealed against being struck off the rolls during the SIR.SC said a chunk of appeals was by those challenging inclusion. EC will give breakup differentiating those seeking inclusion from exclusion. Prioritising inclusion appeals would considerably reduce burden on tribunals, it said.For petitioner Prasenjit Bose from Congress, advocates Gopal Sankaranarayanan and Neha Rathi alleged that bulk of appeals for exclusion/deletion have been filed by EC in a mechanical manner against orders of judicial officers who had directed inclusion of the names and these appeals should not be heard at all.Sankaranarayanan said Kolkata and Howrah civic polls are due in Dec and at least appeals pertaining to these areas should be decided expeditiously so nobody gets disenfranchised illegally.SC said its main concern was expeditious decision on appeals of disenfranchised people. It directed EC to respond with data on appeals pending after segregating them into two categories â those seeking inclusion and those seeking exclusion of names. It asked EC to suggest a mechanism for speeding up disposal, including increasing the number of tribunals.The bench also asked EC to detail steps taken to include names of those whose appeals had been allowed. EC said it was holding meetings with the acting CJ of Calcutta HC and would submit a proposal on expediting disposal.Appearing for some petitioners, advocate Rauf Rahim said people whose names were deleted and whose appeals were pending should not be deprived of ration and benefits under the govt schemes.Advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay told the bench that in Murshidabad, many constituencies had voter deletions far exceeding winning margin, and alleged a particular community appeared to have been targeted through SIR. SC will hear issue again next week.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Aristotle: âThe man of practical wisdom aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure"
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The pursuit of pleasure is often treated as one of life's simplest goals, but Aristotle offered a more measured view of what it means to live wisely. .
articles.body: The pursuit of pleasure is often treated as one of life's simplest goals, but Aristotle offered a more measured view of what it means to live wisely. In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle wrote: âThe man of practical wisdom aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure.â The statement appears in his discussion of pleasure, pain and self-control, where he considers whether pleasure should be treated as the highest good. Aristotle's argument suggests that practical wisdom is not simply about seeking whatever feels good in the moment. Instead, it involves understanding which desires are worth following and recognising when the pursuit of pleasure can ultimately create greater difficulties. His words remain relevant because modern life constantly encourages people to seek comfort, entertainment and immediate satisfaction. The quote offers a reminder that wisdom can sometimes mean choosing what prevents unnecessary pain rather than constantly pursuing what feels pleasurable.Quote of the day by Aristotle: What did Aristotle mean by the quote?Aristotle's statement centres on the difference between practical wisdom and the pursuit of immediate pleasure. In Nicomachean Ethics, he discusses the way people respond to pleasure and pain and examines the behaviour of those who lack self-control. His point is not that all pleasure is bad or that a wise person should live without enjoyment. Instead, Aristotle distinguishes between pleasures that are beneficial and excessive or misguided pleasures that can lead to problems. The practically wise person therefore does not make pleasure the sole objective. Such a person understands that avoiding unnecessary pain can be more important than chasing temporary enjoyment.The idea becomes clearer when considered alongside Aristotle's broader discussion of self-control. He argues that people can become overly driven by pleasurable things and that this pursuit can itself produce pain. Someone who constantly seeks immediate gratification may eventually face consequences that outweigh the original pleasure. Practical wisdom therefore requires judgement. It means considering where a particular choice will lead rather than evaluating it only by how enjoyable it feels in the present. Aristotle's message is ultimately about moderation, foresight and the ability to place short-term desires within the context of a larger and more balanced life.Why avoiding unnecessary pain can be a form of wisdomPeople often associate wisdom with achieving more, gaining more or experiencing more pleasure. Aristotle's observation presents another way of looking at it. Sometimes the wiser decision is the one that prevents avoidable problems from developing in the first place. A person may choose discipline over excess, restraint over impulse or preparation over convenience because these choices can reduce difficulties later. This does not mean avoiding every challenge. Some difficulties are necessary for growth, and Aristotle's wider philosophy places considerable importance on developing good character through practice and habit. The point is to distinguish between worthwhile difficulty and unnecessary suffering. Practical wisdom helps a person recognise that difference and make choices accordingly.This idea remains relevant in everyday decisions. Eating or spending excessively may provide immediate pleasure but create problems later. Avoiding difficult responsibilities may feel comfortable in the moment but increase stress over time. Similarly, constantly choosing entertainment over meaningful work can offer short-term satisfaction while making long-term goals harder to achieve. Aristotle's argument encourages people to look beyond the immediate emotional reward and consider the consequences of their choices.Why chasing pleasure does not always lead to happinessAristotle's discussion is particularly interesting because he does not simply argue that pleasure is worthless. In Nicomachean Ethics, he examines different arguments about pleasure and ultimately treats pleasure as having an important place in human life. His concern is with the assumption that every pleasurable experience should automatically be pursued. Some pleasures can be excessive, harmful or connected to desires that undermine self-control.This distinction is important in a world where instant gratification is increasingly accessible. Entertainment, shopping, food, social media and other forms of stimulation can provide immediate rewards with very little effort. Yet the fact that something is enjoyable does not necessarily mean that pursuing more of it will improve a person's life. Aristotle's idea encourages a more deliberate approach. Instead of asking only whether something feels good, a person can also ask whether it is good for them, whether it supports their goals and whether the consequences are worth the temporary pleasure.Aristotle and the importance of practical wisdomPractical wisdom, or phronesis, occupies an important place in Aristotle's ethical philosophy. It concerns the ability to deliberate well about how to act in particular circumstances. Rather than relying on simple rules, practical wisdom involves judging what is appropriate in a given situation and choosing actions that contribute to a good life. Aristotle's discussion of pleasure and pain forms part of this wider examination of human behaviour, virtue and self-control.The quote therefore should not be interpreted as a simple instruction to avoid discomfort at all costs. A wise person may willingly accept temporary pain or difficulty when it serves a worthwhile purpose. Studying can be difficult, exercise can be uncomfortable and achieving an important goal can require sacrifice. The wisdom lies in understanding which difficulties are meaningful and which forms of pain are simply the consequences of poor choices. Aristotle's approach asks people to think beyond immediate feelings and consider the broader consequences of their actions.The timeless lessonAristotle's words ultimately encourage a more thoughtful relationship with pleasure and pain. A good life is not necessarily one in which every moment is comfortable or every desire is satisfied. Wisdom involves knowing when to pursue something, when to exercise restraint and when avoiding a particular choice can save us from greater difficulties later. The quote reminds us that self-control is not about rejecting pleasure but about refusing to let pleasure control our decisions. In a culture increasingly focused on instant gratification, Aristotle's ancient observation offers a simple but powerful lesson: sometimes the wisest choice is not the one that promises the greatest pleasure, but the one that prevents unnecessary pain and helps us live with greater balance and judgement.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. He argues that people can become overly driven by pleasurable things and that this pursuit can itself produce pain. Someone who constantly seeks immediate gratification may eventually face consequences that outweigh the original pleasure. Practical wisdom therefore requires judgement. It means considering where a particular choice will lead rather than evaluating it only by how enjoyable it feels in the present. Aristotle's message is ultimately about moderation, foresight and the ability to place short-term desires within the context of a larger and more balanced life.Why avoiding unnecessary pain can be a form of wisdomPeople often associate wisdom with achieving more, gaining more or experiencing more pleasure. Aristotle's observation presents another way of looking at it. Sometimes the wiser decision is the one that prevents avoidable problems from developing in the first place. A person may choose discipline over excess, restraint over impulse or preparation over convenience because these choices can reduce difficulties later. This does not mean avoiding every challenge. Some difficulties are necessary for growth, and Aristotle's wider philosophy places considerable importance on developing good character through practice and habit. The point is to distinguish between worthwhile difficulty and unnecessary suffering. Practical wisdom helps a person recognise that difference and make choices accordingly.This idea remains relevant in everyday decisions. Eating or spending excessively may provide immediate pleasure but create problems later. Avoiding difficult responsibilities may feel comfortable in the moment but increase stress over time. Similarly, constantly choosing entertainment over meaningful work can offer short-term satisfaction while making long-term goals harder to achieve. Aristotle's argument encourages people to look beyond the immediate emotional reward and consider the consequences of their choices.Why chasing pleasure does not always lead to happinessAristotle's discussion is particularly interesting because he does not simply argue that pleasure is worthless. In Nicomachean Ethics, he examines different arguments about pleasure and ultimately treats pleasure as having an important place in human life. His concern is with the assumption that every pleasurable experience should automatically be pursued. Some pleasures can be excessive, harmful or connected to desires that undermine self-control.This distinction is important in a world where instant gratification is increasingly accessible. Entertainment, shopping, food, social media and other forms of stimulation can provide immediate rewards with very little effort. Yet the fact that something is enjoyable does not necessarily mean that pursuing more of it will improve a person's life. Aristotle's idea encourages a more deliberate approach. Instead of asking only whether something feels good, a person can also ask whether it is good for them, whether it supports their goals and whether the consequences are worth the temporary pleasure.Aristotle and the importance of practical wisdomPractical wisdom, or phronesis, occupies an important place in Aristotle's ethical philosophy. It concerns the ability to deliberate well about how to act in particular circumstances. Rather than relying on simple rules, practical wisdom involves judging what is appropriate in a given situation and choosing actions that contribute to a good life. Aristotle's discussion of pleasure and pain forms part of this wider examination of human behaviour, virtue and self-control.The quote therefore should not be interpreted as a simple instruction to avoid discomfort at all costs. A wise person may willingly accept temporary pain or difficulty when it serves a worthwhile purpose. Studying can be difficult, exercise can be uncomfortable and achieving an important goal can require sacrifice. The wisdom lies in understanding which difficulties are meaningful and which forms of pain are simply the consequences of poor choices. Aristotle's approach asks people to think beyond immediate feelings and consider the broader consequences of their actions.The timeless lessonAristotle's words ultimately encourage a more thoughtful relationship with pleasure and pain. A good life is not necessarily one in which every moment is comfortable or every desire is satisfied. Wisdom involves knowing when to pursue something, when to exercise restraint and when avoiding a particular choice can save us from greater difficulties later. The quote reminds us that self-control is not about rejecting pleasure but about refusing to let pleasure control our decisions. In a culture increasingly focused on instant gratification, Aristotle's ancient observation offers a simple but powerful lesson: sometimes the wisest choice is not the one that promises the greatest pleasure, but the one that prevents unnecessary pain and helps us live with greater balance and judgement.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Best hiking trails near Scott Stadium in Charlottesville: a guide for Virginia football fans
articles.summary: Before the Cavaliers kick off at Scott Stadium, explore Humpback Rocks, the Blue Hole swimming spot, and Shenandoah National Park all within 35 minutes.
articles.body: Week 0 | NC State at Virginia | Saturday, Aug. 29 | Scott Stadium, Charlottesville, VA | 3:30 p.m. ET Funny how things work out. This game was supposed to be college football's first trip to South America, with NC State and Virginia set to kick off Week 0 at Nilton Santos Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. Then the whole thing fell apart this summer when Athlete Advantage (the event organizer) told the ACC it simply couldn't pull it off. So the Wolfpack and Cavaliers got rerouted back to the far less exotic — but far more practical — Blue Ridge foothills of Charlottesville instead. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Virginia's loss of a trip to Rio is your gain. Instead of fighting for a spot on a flight to Brazil, you can be standing on a mountaintop overlooking the Shenandoah Valley by 9 a.m. and in your tailgate spot by 1. Charlottesville sits right up against the Blue Ridge Parkway and the edge of Shenandoah National Park, which means some of the best hiking in Virginia is closer to Scott Stadium than most fans realize. Here's where to go — all within an hour of kickoff and none requiring a passport or conversational Portuguese. Saunders-Monticello Trail 10 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy The one to bring the whole crew, including grandparents and strollers. A 4.4-mile out-and-back on packed gravel and raised boardwalk, climbing gently through forest canopy up to the visitor center at Thomas Jefferson's Monticello. Dog-friendly, wheelchair-accessible and shaded most of the way. If anyone in your group wants to actually tour the house, that's a separate ticket — $23 to $30 for adults, $10 for kids 5 to 11 — but the trail itself is free. Blue Ridge Tunnel 30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy A change of pace from the usual mountain-view hike: a 4.6-mile out-and-back through an actual 1850s railroad tunnel carved straight through the mountain under Rockfish Gap. Bring a flashlight or headlamp — it gets really dark in there, and the temperature drops the deeper you go, which is an added bonus. BEAT THE HEAT: HERE ARE SOME OF THE BEST TIPS TO AVOID HEATSTROKE DURING A HIKE THIS SUMMER Shenandoah National Park (Rockfish Gap entrance) 25 minutes from Scott Stadium | $30 per vehicle | Moderate If you're only going to spend money on one thing this weekend besides the game, this is the one worth it. The Rockfish Gap entrance drops you right onto Skyline Drive, with two standout hikes an easy detour apart: Calvary and Chimney Rocks at milepost 90, a short trek out to a flat-topped rock overlook, and Turk Mountain at milepost 93.5, which delivers rock scrambles and real mountain views for the effort. Being a national park, it will cost you an entry fee of $30 per vehicle, which is good for seven days. Sugar Hollow Reservoir & the Blue Hole 35 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate The pick if you’re looking to do a little soaking. A 3-mile out-and-back from the Sugar Hollow parking area leads to the Blue Hole, a genuinely beautiful swimming hole on the Moormans River. This spot keeps showing up on the "best swimming holes in Virginia" lists for a reason. Bring water shoes; the rocks get slick. If your crew wants more of a workout instead, a separate 4.6-mile route from the same lot heads out to Big Branch Falls through a shaded forest. Humpback Rocks 30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate-strenuous The payoff hike, and the one most worth setting an alarm for. It's a brutal, steep mile straight up, but the reward is a 360-degree view across the Shenandoah Valley and Blue Ridge that's tough to beat anywhere in the state. This is the one hike on the list with zero shade at the top, so this is the one to knock out at sunrise, not after brunch. Sunrise at Humpback is a bucket-list item for many UVA students. Crabtree Falls 60–75 minutes from Scott Stadium | $3 day-use fee | Moderate-strenuous Crabtree Falls is a series of five major cascades tumbling a total of 1,200 feet down the mountainside. For context, that's taller than the Eiffel Tower. And the longest single cascade in that series drops 400 feet, enough to make Crabtree Falls the tallest single vertical-drop waterfall east of the Mississippi. The hike up alongside it is a 3-mile round trip with switchbacks and handrails at the steeper spots. It's genuinely one of the most photographed trails in Virginia. The catch: this one runs 60 to 75 minutes from Scott Stadium depending on route and traffic. If you're rolling into Charlottesville just for the game, Crabtree probably isn't the move. But if you're making a weekend of it and have an extra day before or after, it's worth the drive. We should probably also mention there's another Crabtree Falls off the Blue Ridge Parkway in North Carolina. Make sure you're plugging the right one into your GPS. Truthfully, you can't go wrong no matter which trail you choose. Between the Blue Ridge Parkway, Shenandoah National Park and a reservoir system that seems to have a trail wrapped around every corner of it, Charlottesville is about as good as it gets for outdoor adventurers who also happen to love college football. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Every week this season, OutKick OutDoors is finding the best ways to touch grass before you touch down at the tailgate. Got a favorite spot near your campus we should know about? Hit us up on Instagram and TikTok.

articles.title: A Pittsburgh school went from 130 fights per year to 10, using an idea from ‘Harry Potter’
articles.summary: A school in Pittsburgh nearly eliminated its violence problem by, in part, implementing a school house system a la Harry Potter.
articles.body:
Pittsburgh Arlington PreK-8 public school had a major behavior problem on its hands. With just 360 students enrolled, the school saw more than 130 fights in the 2024-25 school year. Many of the kids who weren't suspended for violence were chronically absent.

The school also couldn't hold on to a principal , going through four in just a couple of years.

Finally, school leadership decided to take action.

Principal and staff begin making major changes

Principal Crystal Caldwell and her leadership staff knew they had to do something. The reputation of the school had reached rock bottom.

"Arlington's history has been a school of violence, and 'Oh, don't send your kid there,'" she told TribLive .

Step one was increasing communication. Caldwell and supporting staff began having "safety huddles" every morning with teachers in order to identify potential conflicts before they exploded into physical fights.

Some days that might mean pulling an irritable student aside for counseling or keeping a watchful eye out for kids who are showing signs of struggling at home. All of the staff banded together to keep these little problems from boiling over.

They also began leaning into a concept known as "restorative practices." Whenever possible, it replaces traditional punishments like detention and suspension with actions that help repair the harm the student caused in the school community. A student might have to clean the hallway if they vandalized it, or apologize and talk it out when they've had a conflict with another student.

"We let the kids talk it out, and they come up with their own way to apologize and say how they will do better," Caldwell told TribLive. "They need a moment of knowing it's OK to make mistakes, but knowing they can learn from it."

But perhaps the most interesting change Caldwell and her team enacted was ripped right out of the pages of Harry Potter .

Harry Potter -inspired 'house' system builds community among students

In Harry Potter , students at the magical wizarding school of Hogwarts are sorted into houses upon their arrival—Hufflepuff, Slytherin, Ravenclaw, and of course, Gryffindor. It's like a little team with its very own mascot, virtues, and color scheme. Students can earn or lose points for their house throughout the year in an epic competition with the other houses.

It's an idea taken from real-life British boarding schools , and it's now making its way into American public schools as evidenced by Pittsburgh Arlington.

The house system builds community and belonging for students. Competing against the other houses via good behavior also creates a built-in reward system that the students love.

After 130 fights at Pittsburgh Arlington in 2024, last school year there were only 10. That's right, just 10 fights after implementing safety huddles, the house system, and other changes. That's an absolutely incredible turnaround for a school that was on the brink.

House system is making a difference in schools all over the country

Houses have been so effective in Pittsburgh that the public school district is now rolling the program out to dozens of schools.

It's also being used in nearby Duquesne City Schools where the district has reported a 74% drop in student disciplinary incidents since implementing houses.

Union County public schools in North Carolina are utilizing a similar system at about a dozen elementary schools. And that's not even including the many individual schools around the country that are taking matters into their own hands to try out the clever idea from the wizarding world.

There are a lot of mechanisms hidden inside the house system that make it incredibly effective at engaging students. For starters, all kids find a sense of belonging and loyalty to their house just by the simple act of being sorted. Students are sorted into houses across different grades, so a natural mentorship arrangement often arises where older students can help younger students. Positive, pro-social behavior also becomes gamified via friendly competition.

Having a house system has been shown to reduce bullying, lower the number of fights and suspensions, and even improve academic performance across the board.

When students are experiencing homelessness or extreme poverty, violence in the streets on which they live, hunger, and more, they often act out and struggle in school.

But along with other schools around the country, Pittsburgh Arlington is proving that it's still possible to make school a safe, welcoming place even when the world outside is anything but—and that can make all the difference.

articles.title: Back to school: How to save on uniform costs
articles.summary: From baby banks to supermarket deals, there are many ways parents can ease the back-to-school burden.
articles.body:
Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs it brings.

Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.

And a third of the 2,000 parents polled said they've sacrificed things for themselves to meet back-to-school costs like uniforms, bags or books.

New rules limiting the number of items branded with a school logo to three per child come into force in September, aimed at helping ease the financial burden.

From baby banks to council grants, here are ways parents can ease the cost of kitting out their kids for school.

Save the Children said the new uniform rules are a "good start" but back-to-school costs remain a concern for families across almost all income brackets.

The government said schools should make second-hand uniforms accessible to parents.

"Speak to a teacher you trust, and explain that the costs are difficult," said Megan Meek-O'Connor, head of England and Westminster at Save the Children.

Many schools have uniform hubs, swap shops and sales just before term starts, and hardship funds.

In London, the School Uniform Reuse Network launched earlier this year, giving schools practical advice to start or improve their own swap shops.

During its first term of operation, it saw more than 1,500 items reused across 24 schools.

Parents of older children may not realise a so-called baby bank can help them, but many of the 400 support hubs across the UK provide uniforms for children up to and through secondary school.

In its latest survey of members, the Baby Bank Alliance found school uniform was reported as a priority item for the first time.

Late summer is one of the busiest times for Little Stars Shrewsbury - just over half the children helped since June have been given uniform support.

Hannah Stoddart, operations manager at Little Stars Shrewsbury, said families come to them in varying circumstances. A child starting school might need fully kitting out, while an older pupil may just need to replace one or two items.

Stoddart stressed that while the summer holidays "take their toll", the charity provides help all year.

"So when they've had that growth spurt, when they've scuffed their shoes or they've ripped their trousers or they need a winter coat, that's something they can come back to us for as well," she said.

The relaxed rules on uniform branding mean parents can purchase more items from supermarkets and charity shops, said Save the Children's Meek-O'Connor.

Pre-loved items are usually what "kids have grown out of quickly rather than things that are poor quality", she said.

Parents can cheaply stock up on frequent-wear items with supermarket bundle deals, while the charity Family Action suggested they team up to bulk buy items that would otherwise take them over budget.

According to research from the bank Nationwide, a third of parents said they buy uniform from supermarkets, a third shop around for the best value and 23% purchase larger sizes so items last longer.

Kate Steere, parent and consumer editor at the comparison site Finder, said sports kit costs can be "brutal".

"I always encourage parents to tap into their club's community. Families with older kids are usually eager to pass down gear," she said.

"My boys' football team runs a summer sale for second-hand kit, and apps like Vinted or Facebook Marketplace are goldmines."

You may be able to get a grant from your local authority if your income is below a certain threshold or you're receiving certain benefits.

These can be worth up to £200 per child.

Eligibility and how much you can get can vary according to where in the UK you live, so it is best to check with your council directly.

Struggling with uniform costs is common and people shouldn't feel ashamed if they need to ask for help, said Meek-O'Connor.

"Uniform is supposed to be about making school kind of more accessible, more equal... it should be something positive," she said.

articles.title: L.A. takes aim at phenibut, an unregulated 'gas station drug' that is growing in popularity
articles.summary: L.A. City Council hopes to regulate phenibut, a drug one councilmember says is widely available to children in gas stations and convenience stores.
articles.body:
Los Angeles is looking to regulate another "gas station drug" on commercial shelves.

In a unanimous vote Tuesday, the L.A. City Council instructed the City Attorney to draft new regulations for phenibut, a Cold War-era drug that is said to have been used by Soviet cosmonauts, but abused now as a central nervous system depressant.

Regulations will include restricting sales to people under 21, banning sales near schools and daycare centers and the creation of labels warning against its use, according to the motion .

The full council must vote again on ordinance language before the regulations become law.

"Phenibut is a powerful, unregulated substance that has been sold openly to kids at gas stations and convenience stores across our city, with no age restrictions and little warning of its risks. That ends now," said Councilmember Heather Hutt, who authored the motion.

Nina Paquette, a Marlborough High School senior, brought the existence of the drug and its dangers to Hutt's attention.

"The drug is often marketed directly to children, who are able to purchase it easily without any age restrictions," Hutt said. "Our young people are at extreme risk of developing a severe dependence on this easily accessible substance."

Phenibut is not federally regulated and cannot be legally sold as a dietary supplement. Despite that, Hutt said, it's easily available in L.A. convenience stores.

Paquette, a former intern for state Assemblymember John Harabedian (D-Pasadena), said phenibut pills are often marketed as "smart drugs" or "brain boosters" on social media.

"Teenagers can buy it at gas stations with no idea it can cause addiction, seizures, hallucinations, psychosis and coma," Paquette said.

In Russia, phenibut is a prescription drug used to treat anxiety, insomnia, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and other ailments. It functions much like Valium or Xanax by depressing the central nervous system, and has been banned in several countries and Utah .

According to some studies , phenibut can be addictive and cause withdrawal symptoms. Studies looking into poison control reports found it can lead to trouble breathing , coma or death. Researchers warn that it is an up-and-coming drug that western medicine knows little about.

It's not the first time an unregulated gas station drug has come under fire in L.A.

The Southeast Asian plant kratom and its alternate powerful synthetic alkaloid 7-OH, another drug that escaped federal regulation for years and regularly sold in gas stations and smoke shops, was linked to six overdose deaths across L.A. County last year.

Kratom was temporarily deemed a scheduled substance by the FDA and has been pulled from shelves across California , according to Governor Gavin Newsom.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .
